title: How to Find Broken Links and Fix Them Before They Cost You Traffic

content_html:
You click a link in your own navigation and land on a "Page not found" message. Or a customer emails to say the "Download our price list" button goes nowhere. Either way, you have just met a broken link, and it is rarely the only one. The quickest way to find broken links is to stop waiting for visitors to report them and check the whole site at once.

Broken links build up quietly. Pages get renamed, products get retired, a blog post you linked to five years ago disappears, and nobody updates the links that pointed at them. On a site of any size, a few dead links per year turns into dozens.

This guide explains the different kinds of broken links, why they matter for visitors and search engines, how to find them with a crawl and in Google Search Console, and a simple decision tree for fixing each one. It is the status code step of our technical SEO audit for small sites, covered in full.

What counts as a broken link

A broken link is any link whose destination does not return a working page. The status code the server sends back is what tells you whether a link is broken, not how the page looks. The usual suspects:

  • 404 Not Found: the URL does not exist. By far the most common.
  • 410 Gone: the page was removed on purpose.
  • 5xx server errors: the server failed to produce the page, either briefly or every time.
  • Timeouts and DNS failures: the domain no longer exists or never answers, which is common with links to old external sites.
  • Soft 404s: the page says "not found" or is empty, but the server still returns 200 OK. These look fine to a basic checker and are easy to miss.

It also helps to separate links by where they live:

  • Internal broken links point from one page on your site to another page on your site. You control both ends, so these are the easiest to fix and the most important.
  • Outbound broken links point from your site to someone else's. You cannot fix their page, but you can fix your link.
  • Inbound links to dead pages are links on other sites that point at a URL you removed. You cannot edit their link, but you can decide what that URL does now.

Broken images, scripts and stylesheets follow the same logic. A missing image file is a broken link inside your page, even if no visitor ever clicks it.

Why broken links matter

A single dead link will not sink a site. Google is clear that 404s on some URLs do not count against the rest. Its post on whether 404 errors hurt your site says the fact that some URLs return 404 does not affect how your other, working URLs perform in search results. So this is not about a penalty. It is about three practical costs.

1. Broken crawl paths

Search engines find pages by following links. Google's link best practices describe links as a way to find new pages to crawl and a signal of relevance. When your only internal link to a page is broken, you have cut the path to it. When a menu link is broken, every page that uses that menu repeats the dead end.

2. Lost visitor trust

A visitor who hits a dead end on your site usually does not hunt for the right page. They hit back. On a checkout path, a booking flow or a "Contact us" link, that is a lost lead, not just a bad impression.

3. Wasted link value

If other sites link to a page you deleted, those links now point at nothing. The visitors they send land on an error, and any value those links carried is not reaching a live page. Earning those links in the first place is the hard part, as our guide to earning backlinks and authority explains, so letting them go to waste is an expensive mistake.

Say you run a garden center site and you retire a popular "How to plant spring bulbs" page during a redesign. Local newsletters and a gardening forum link to it. After the redesign, every one of those links ends on a 404, and the internal "Seasonal tips" box on twenty product pages does too.

How to find broken links on your site

Use two sources, because each catches things the other misses. A crawl shows you what is broken right now and which page links to it. Search Console shows you what Google has actually tried to fetch, including old URLs that only external sites still link to.

Crawl your site

A site crawler starts at your home page, follows every link the way a search engine does, and records the status code of each URL it finds. The useful output is not just the broken URL but the pages that link to it, because that is where you make the fix.

A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags 4xx and 5xx pages, broken links and images, and pages that link to non-200 URLs, then exports the list to CSV. Whatever tool you use, check a few things:

  • Turn on checking for external URLs if your tool supports it, so outbound links are tested too.
  • Sort by status code and group the results by broken URL. One dead page linked from 40 places is one fix in a template, not 40.
  • Recheck outbound "broken" links by hand before you change them. Some sites return 403 or 429 to automated requests while working fine in a browser.

Check the Page indexing report in Search Console

In Search Console, open Indexing, then Pages, and look under the reasons pages are not indexed. Two statuses matter here, and Google's Page indexing report documentation explains both:

  • Not found (404): Google requested the URL and got a 404. Google says it may have found the URL through a link from another page, or the page existed and was deleted. It also notes that a 404 is not necessarily a problem if the page was removed with no replacement, and that a moved page should get a 301.
  • Soft 404: the page looks like an error to Google but returns 200. Google recommends returning a real 404 status for pages that truly do not exist.

Click a URL in either list and use URL Inspection to see more detail, including how Google discovered it. Expect old URLs here that your own site no longer links to. Those usually come from external links or old sitemaps, which is exactly what a crawl of your own site cannot show you.

Find external links pointing at dead pages

The Links report in Search Console lists your top linked pages from other sites. Export that list and check the status code of each URL. Any URL that has external links but now returns 404 is a page worth redirecting, because people may still be arriving there.

How to fix broken links: a decision tree

Every broken link has two ends: the link and the destination. Ask these questions in order and stop at the first "yes".

  1. Is the link simply wrong? A typo, a missing slash, or an old URL after a rename. Update the link so it points straight at the correct live URL.
  2. Should the page still exist? If it was deleted by accident, or still gets traffic and links, restore it at its original URL.
  3. Is there a close equivalent? If the content moved or merged into another page, add a 301 redirect from the old URL to that page, then update your internal links to point at the new URL directly. Our guide to choosing between 301 and 302 redirects covers which code to use and how to avoid chains.
  4. Is it gone for good, with no replacement? Let the URL return 404 or 410 and remove or replace every internal link to it.

Two rules keep this honest. First, do not redirect every dead URL to your home page. A visitor who wanted a specific article and lands on the home page is no better off than with a 404, and an unrelated destination does not tell Google where the content went.

Second, 404 and 410 are close enough that you do not need to worry much about which one to use. Google's documentation on how status codes affect its crawlers says all 4xx errors except 429 are treated the same, and that URLs already in the index are removed once they return a 4xx.

For outbound links the tree is shorter, because you only control your end:

  • Search the other site for the new location of the page and update your link.
  • If it is gone, link to another reliable source that backs the same point.
  • If no replacement exists and the sentence still makes sense without it, remove the link.

Fix the source, not just the symptom

A redirect catches old bookmarks and links from other sites. It should not be how your own navigation works. If your menu links to a URL that redirects, every visit and every crawl takes an extra hop to reach a page you control.

After any fix, update the places that point at the old URL:

  • Navigation, footer and sidebar templates, where one change fixes every page.
  • Body links in posts and pages.
  • Canonical tags that reference the old URL.
  • Your XML sitemap. A sitemap that still lists deleted pages sends Google back to them, so keep your sitemap in sync with what actually exists.

Then recrawl. Your list of broken links and internal redirects should shrink to zero, apart from anything you deliberately left as a 404.

Build a custom 404 page that helps

Some 404s are unavoidable. People mistype URLs and old links live on for years. A good custom 404 page turns that dead end into a detour.

A useful 404 page:

  • Says plainly that the page could not be found, without jargon.
  • Uses the same header, navigation and styling as the rest of the site.
  • Offers a search box and links to your main sections or most popular pages.
  • Gives a way to report the problem if the visitor followed a link on your site.

The technical catch: a custom 404 page must still return a 404 status code. If your server sends 200 with a "not found" message, you have created soft 404s. Check with a terminal by requesting a URL you know does not exist:

curl -I https://example.com/this-page-does-not-exist

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

If you see HTTP/1.1 200 OK instead, fix the server or CMS setting so missing pages return a real 404. Also watch for "page not found" templates that some themes serve with a 200 for empty category or search pages.

Keep broken links from coming back

Fixing broken links once is satisfying. Keeping the count near zero takes a small habit, not a big project.

  • Before you delete or rename a page, check which pages link to it and decide on the redirect at the same time.
  • After a redesign, migration or CMS change, crawl the site the same day and compare against the previous crawl.
  • On a schedule, crawl monthly for an active site or quarterly for a small, stable one, and check the Page indexing report in between.
  • For outbound links, prefer linking to stable pages, such as official documentation, over pages likely to move.

Broken links on other people's sites can also be an opportunity. Finding dead links on relevant pages and offering your own content as a replacement is a link building technique in its own right, but that is outreach, and a separate job from cleaning up your own site.

The bottom line

To find broken links, combine a crawl of your site with the Page indexing report in Search Console. The crawl shows you which of your pages contain dead links. Search Console shows you which old URLs Google and other sites still try to reach.

Fix each one in order: correct the link, restore the page, redirect to the closest equivalent, or let it 404 cleanly. Then update your templates and sitemap so your own site never relies on a redirect, and make sure your 404 page returns a real 404.

Your next step: crawl your site today, export every URL that returns a 4xx or 5xx along with the pages that link to it, and fix the broken links in your navigation and templates first.

faqs.question: Do broken links hurt SEO?
faqs.answer: Not directly as a penalty. Google has said that 404s on some URLs do not affect how your working URLs perform. The real costs are indirect: broken internal links cut the paths crawlers use to find pages, visitors leave, and backlinks pointing at dead pages stop reaching a live page.

faqs.question: How often should I check my site for broken links?
faqs.answer: A monthly crawl suits an active site that publishes or changes pages often, and a quarterly crawl is usually enough for a small, stable site. Always run an extra crawl straight after a redesign, migration or bulk URL change, because that is when broken links appear in large numbers.

faqs.question: Should I redirect all 404 pages to my home page?
faqs.answer: No. Redirect a dead URL only when there is a genuinely close equivalent page. Sending every missing page to the home page leaves visitors no better off than a 404 and does not tell Google where the content went. If there is no replacement, let the URL return 404 or 410.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 404 and a soft 404?
faqs.answer: A 404 is a real HTTP status code telling browsers and crawlers that the page does not exist. A soft 404 is a page that looks like an error or is empty but returns a 200 OK status. Google reports soft 404s in Search Console and recommends returning a real 404 status for pages that do not exist.

faqs.question: Is a 410 better than a 404 for deleted pages?
faqs.answer: For Google it makes little practical difference. Google's documentation says it treats all 4xx errors except 429 the same way and removes already indexed URLs that return them. Use 410 if you want to state clearly that removal was deliberate, but a 404 is perfectly fine.
